extracted.intended_audience: Patent office examiners, policymakers, and patent applicants/stakeholders in ASEAN Member States
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for patentable subject matter, examination procedures, oppositions, appeals, and accelerated prosecution programmes applicable in ASEAN Member States. Covers exclusions from patentability, substantive examination content, third-party submissions, and best practices for opposition systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of regional and bilateral PPH programmes
rubrics_metrics.description: ASEAN Member States operate ASPEC PPH programmes (ASPEC Prosecution Highway, PCT-ASPEC, ASPEC for Industry 4.0 Infrastructure and Manufacturing) and have entered into bilateral PPH arrangements to expedite examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These programmes can be paired with each other and with national PPH schemes to further expedite examination and grant of patents. See Chapter 14 “Work sharing” for programme details and differing levels of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: National fast-track/acceleration programmes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AMS (Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore) provide domestic fast track programmes to expedite examination and grant of patents, with country-specific conditions, caps and expected grant timelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Singapore launched a program (from 4 May 2020) allowing 10 applications/month with per-entity caps; Thailand pilot requires applicant reasons and limits claims and monthly acceptances; Malaysia has tech-field based provision. Conditions commonly require applicants to state reasons for expedited examination and may impose claim limits, caps per month, applicant residency/filing conditions and response deadlines. Expected grant timelines (where specified) may be under 12 months or as short as 1 week after clear S&E report for some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of patentable subject matter during substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter should normally be assessed during substantive examination by examiners well versed in patentability conditions (exception noted for Viet Nam which assesses in both formality and substantive examination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because assessment of patentability is usually complex, it is recommended that highly knowledgeable examiners perform it in substantive examination rather than in formality checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of substantive examination reports to third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive examination report should be made available to third parties at the latest after the granting date of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice is to make substantive examination reports available to third parties to support transparency and post-grant scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant right to respond to substantive examination objections
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner issues an objection, the applicant must be allowed to file a response (explanation, data, evidence) suitable for addressing the objections; admission of the response depends on the individual case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner upholds the rejection after considering the response, the applicant may appeal to an upper administrative body or competent court. Example: where an adverse S&E report gives applicant 3 weeks to respond; failure to respond may result in deemed withdrawal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedures against substantive examination decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Following receipt of the substantive examination report, the applicant may file an appeal against a decision rejecting a patent through administrative and judicial procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals should be available against decisions rejecting applications; specific procedures and timelines depend on national law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum content of a substantive examination report
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantive examination report should minimally include: assessment of patentability of the invention; search report (if applicable); list and details of cited prior art including patent and non-patent literature; grounds for rejecting the application and explanation; deadline to respond to an objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The language is normally the official language of filing; some offices outsource and produce reports in English; Brunei, Philippines, Malaysia and Singapore generally produce examination reports in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition actions provide early third-party review
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-grant and post-grant opposition actions allow third parties to oppose grant of a patent by alleging at least one ground (e.g., lack of novelty) and submitting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposition proceedings are generally inter partes before the patent office, intended to be simple, fast and inexpensive mechanisms to ensure quality and validity of granted patents and allow early rectification of invalid patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-grant opposition procedural elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-grant opposition may be filed after publication of the application within prescribed time periods; opponents must state grounds, submit evidence and pay fees; applicant is notified and may respond within prescribed time limits; examiner decides based on submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some AMS, pre-grant opposition begins after positive formality examination. Publication of application (e.g., after 18 months) or grant is a prerequisite for opposition in many jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant opposition procedural elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-grant opposition allows third parties to challenge a granted patent within statutory deadlines after grant; submissions including evidence are considered, applicant/patentee is notified and may respond; examiner decides whether to maintain, amend or revoke the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some jurisdictions (e.g., Singapore), third parties may apply to revoke a patent or request re-examination; enforceability of opposed patents is uncertain during the opposition period; post-grant opposition does not delay grant timing for patents not subject to opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-practice goals for opposition systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition systems should provide a simple, fast and inexpensive mechanism to ensure quality and validity of granted patents by enabling early rectification of invalid patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance is required: pre-grant opposition increases legal certainty but delays grants broadly; post-grant opposition limits delay to affected patents but creates enforceability uncertainty. Combining both can increase quality but also delay and uncertainty; offices should consider trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public access to full application/granted patent content
rubrics_metrics.description: Best practice is for patent offices to make available to the public the full content of applications or granted patents for inspection to enable effective pre- or post-grant opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope of published information varies by AMS; making full content available facilitates third-party identification of prior art and submission of objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to prior art information for oppositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents should have access to prior art information to support opposition proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access assists opponents in substantiating grounds such as lack of novelty or inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable opposition timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition timeframes should be reasonable and balance interests of applicants/patentees and third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeframes should allow effective participation without unduly prolonging uncertainty or delaying grant processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural formalities enabling effective inter partes opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition procedures should permit conduct of inter partes proceedings, including written and/or oral proceedings, and set rules for provision of supporting evidence and arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear rules on admissibility, evidence submission, and procedural conduct improve fairness and effectiveness of oppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for opposition should balance patent quality and legal certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounds for opposition should be framed to balance the interests of maintaining patent quality and providing legal certainty to rights-holders and third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common grounds include lack of patentability, novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, lack of disclosure/support, incorrect amendments, and applicant eligibility (varies by country).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules on interplay between opposition procedures and invalidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition systems should define the interrelationship between opposition procedures and invalidation/cancellation mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity on when to use opposition vs other invalidation actions and the effect of each on enforceability and appeal rights is important for stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of applicant/patentee to counterclaim and appeal opposition decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants/patentees must have opportunities to file counterclaims to oppositions and to appeal patent office decisions before upper administrative and judicial authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 62.5 TRIPS requires that final administrative decisions regarding acquisition and maintenance of IP rights be subject to judicial/quasi-judicial review; note some third-party observations are non-inter partes and therefore not appealable in certain AMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for opposition (enumerated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible grounds for pre- and post-grant opposition include: (1) claimed invention is not patentable; (2) lacks novelty; (3) lacks inventive step; (4) lacks industrial applicability; additionally, lack of disclosure/support, incorrect amendments and applicant eligibility are grounds in some countries (Indonesia, Lao PDR, Singapore, Viet Nam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents must state grounds and provide supporting evidence (e.g., prior art documents) within prescribed times and fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties entitled to file opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person/party is allowed to file an opposition action; opponents are not necessarily limited to 'interested parties' in jurisdictions that permit broad access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting any person promotes public participation but procedures must balance potential for abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to withdraw opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: An opponent must be able to withdraw its opposition at any time during the proceedings before issuance of the patent office's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal rights provide flexibility for opponents and can affect proceedings duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of foreign patent office decisions in opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition procedures should allow parties to consider decisions issued by foreign offices on oppositions for the same inventions as part of the arguments in opposition proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign decisions are admissible as part of arguments but weight given depends on national practice and case circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party observations during substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party observations may be filed before and during substantive examination, with or without disclosure of identity, to help identify prior art and orient search/examination at an early stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such observations can guide examiners toward relevant prior art; rules on anonymity and admissibility vary by AMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'invention' for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Invention' is what is specified in the claim(s) and in most AMS is defined as a solution to a technical problem producing a technical effect; inventions may be products, processes or product-by-process and may include improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'improvement' need not be better than prior art but can be an alternative providing similar effects. If subject matter does not meet the legal definition of invention, the application may be rejected without examination of other grounds (Singapore treats the assessment together with other grounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of technical character/technical effect for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To be statutory subject-matter an invention must have technical character: relate to a technical field, address a technical problem and have technical features by which protection is defined; one technical feature in a claim can be sufficient for eligibility (assessment made without reference to prior art, except Singapore).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mixed claims, examiners should identify which features contribute to technical character; features non-technical in isolation may contribute to technical character in context if they produce a technical effect serving a technical purpose. Example: use of a smartphone can provide technical character to a claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter: discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: AMS (except Brunei) explicitly prohibit discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods from patentability 'as such'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discoveries are abstract/no technical effect (but practical applications of discoveries may be patentable). Scientific theories as abstract concepts are unpatentable unless applied to produce a technical effect. Mathematical theories and purely abstract methods (e.g., shortcut method of division) are excluded, though machines implementing them may be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter: schemes, rules or methods for doing business, purely mental acts, or playing games
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of doing business, purely mental acts and game rules 'as such' are excluded from patentability because they are abstract and do not produce technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims specify technical means (e.g., a programmable apparatus) executing some steps, the claim may not be excluded. Examples: a computer-implemented method for a business-related function with practical application may be patentable; a pure scheme for organizing a commercial operation would be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter: aesthetic creations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic creations are excluded 'as such' due to lack of industrial applicability or technical effect, but if an aesthetic creation produces a technical effect or includes technical aspects (e.g., substrate and technical function) it may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tyre tread pattern may be a technical feature if it improves water channeling; colour of a tyre sidewall serving only aesthetic purpose would be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter: presentation of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation of information 'as such' (content, displays, acoustical signals, spoken words) is excluded from patentability unless the presentation has technical character or is structurally/ functionally related to an information carrier, process or apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere arrangements/compilations of data are generally excluded unless the presentation has technical character (e.g., gramophone groove form enabling stereo, diapositive with soundtrack). Program listings per se are excluded; data structures embodied in a tangible medium with technical character may be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter: inventions contrary to public order, morality, peace or security
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions likely to induce riot, public disorder, criminal or offensive behaviour are excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is invoked rarely; apply a fairness test whether the public would regard the invention as so abhorrent that granting a patent would be inconceivable (example: a suicide machine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer programs excluded 'as such' but patentable if producing technical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer programs as sequences of executable instructions are abstract and excluded 'as such'. However, inventions implemented by a computer program that produce a technical effect beyond normal physical interactions of software and hardware are not excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal electricity flow in execution is insufficient. Examples of technical effects: controlling anti-lock brakes, emissions determination by X-ray device, video compression, image restoration, encryption, security measures protecting boot integrity. Claims must include essential technical features; product, process and use claims may be allowable once technical character established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-step approach for assessing computer program patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: One approach to determine whether a claimed contribution from a computer program is patentable: (1) properly construe the claim; (2) identify the actual contribution made by the invention; (3) determine whether the actual contribution falls solely within excluded subject matter 'as such'; (4) determine whether the contribution is technical in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should objectively investigate actual contribution (not be bound by applicant's assertion). If technical character is found, proceed to examine novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented inventions are not per se excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'computer-implemented invention' (features implemented by computer programs on programmable apparatus) is primarily intended to cover claims involving computers/networks where at least one feature is implemented by a computer program; claims to computer-implemented methods cannot be objected to as non-patentable subject matter solely for being methods involving technical means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between a computer program (sequence of instructions) and a computer-implemented method (method performed on a computer). Technical means give technical character to methods; computer programs must be drafted to include technical features essential for the technical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery, therapy or diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery, therapy or diagnosis are excluded from patentability to ensure medical/veterinary practitioners are not hindered in exercising professional skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therapeutic instruments/apparatus and products/substances for use in therapeutic methods are not excluded. Treatments that are purely cosmetic may be patentable; chemical contraception is not considered therapeutic. A method that cures/prevents/alleviates disease constitutes therapy whether performed by patient, practitioner or automated system.
